Each teammate must create the same file under their own home directory, since project-level files stay private to their author.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the correct statement plus the two mirror-image misconceptions (CLAUDE.md cannot hold team standards, and project-level files are private) that the hierarchy actually rules out.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that .claude/rules/ is mandatory for anything a team shares; rules files are an option for modularization and path scoping, not a replacement for project-level CLAUDE.md.
distractorRationale.c: Probes an inverted reading of the hierarchy, where project-level files are private and only home-directory copies count as shared.

explanation.correct: The hierarchy has three levels: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project-level (.claude/CLAUDE.md or a root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level subdirectory CLAUDE.md files. Only the project- and directory-level files travel with the repository, so a standard written into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md stays on that one machine. Move it into the project's CLAUDE.md so it is committed and shared.

whyWrong.a: CLAUDE.md is exactly where universal, always-loaded standards belong, and project-level CLAUDE.md files are shared with the team. .claude/rules/ exists to split a large CLAUDE.md into focused topic files or to scope conventions to matching paths - it is not a requirement for team standards.
whyWrong.c: This reverses the guide's diagnosis. Instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are personal and unsent; project-level files are the ones shared with teammates through version control, so no per-teammate home-directory copies are needed.

explanation.analogy: A CLAUDE.md in your home directory is a sticky note on your own monitor; the project's CLAUDE.md is the checklist committed to the repository.
explanation.takeaway: Personal instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md never reach your teammates - team standards belong in the project-level CLAUDE.md.
explanation.deepDive: When behavior looks inconsistent across sessions, the guide points to the /memory command for verifying which memory files are actually loaded.

questions.prompt: Each package in a monorepo is owned by a different maintainer team, and the standards files should stay in one place rather than being duplicated into every package's CLAUDE.md. Which approach does the guide describe?

options.text: Copy the full standards document into every package CLAUDE.md so each package remains self-contained.
Put the standards in one directory-level CLAUDE.md so every package in the repository picks it up.
Turn the standards into a slash command in .claude/commands/ that each package invokes whenever it needs them.
Use @import in each package's CLAUDE.md to reference the external standards files relevant to that package.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because this is a best-choice question about keeping one copy of a standard while loading it selectively. Copying it into every package, parking it in a single directory-level file, and turning it into a command are the three realistic wrong turns; only @import states the standard once and pulls it in where it is relevant.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the copy-everywhere instinct; it works but is exactly the duplication @import exists to remove.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that a directory-level CLAUDE.md broadcasts repository-wide; directory-level files are scoped to their own subdirectory.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusion between on-demand commands and always-loaded standards; a convention that must always apply cannot depend on someone remembering to invoke it.

explanation.correct: @import lets a CLAUDE.md reference external files, which is how the guide describes keeping CLAUDE.md modular: each package's maintainers decide which standards files are relevant to that package and import only those, rather than duplicating the text.

whyWrong.a: That is the duplication @import is designed to avoid - the standard would have to be maintained in N places and would drift between packages.
whyWrong.c: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are scoped to their own subdirectory. They are not a repository-wide broadcast mechanism, so a file in the standards folder would not load for a package elsewhere in the tree.
whyWrong.d: Custom commands are on-demand invocations. Standards that must apply universally belong in CLAUDE.md, which is always loaded.

explanation.analogy: CLAUDE.md is a resume; @import is the 'references available on request' line that avoids pasting every document inline.
explanation.takeaway: @import keeps CLAUDE.md modular: one copy of a standard, imported only by the packages that need it.
explanation.deepDive: Modularization and scoping are complementary: @import keeps one copy of a standard in one place, and .claude/rules/ topic files keep any single CLAUDE.md small enough for a maintainer to read.

questions.prompt: Behavior differs between sessions on the same machine and the team cannot tell which memory files were loaded. Which combination of steps does the guide describe?

options.text: Copy ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md into the repository root so every session loads the identical memory files.
Move every convention into a custom slash command so each convention is only loaded when a developer requests it.
Run /memory to verify which files are loaded, and keep large CLAUDE.md files split into .claude/rules/ topic files.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one correct diagnostic-and-organization pairing, plus the two wrong reflexes - copying personal memory into the repo, and converting standards into on-demand commands.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that /memory-style verification is about file location; the guide's diagnostic is checking which files are loaded, not relocating them.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between diagnosing memory loading and restructuring conventions as commands; commands are on-demand, not part of the memory diagnostic.

explanation.correct: The guide names /memory as the way to verify which memory files are loaded and to diagnose inconsistent behavior across sessions, and separately recommends splitting large CLAUDE.md files into focused topic-specific files in .claude/rules/ - testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md - as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md.

whyWrong.a: Copying the personal file into the repository does not verify what was loaded; it just moves content and blurs the user-level / project-level boundary described in the hierarchy.
whyWrong.c: Commands are invoked on demand by a developer. That is a reorganization choice, not a diagnostic, and it changes universal standards into opt-in behavior.

explanation.takeaway: Use /memory to see what loaded, and use .claude/rules/ to keep a big CLAUDE.md from becoming a monolith.
explanation.deepDive: Diagnosing hierarchy issues and modularizing content are two different jobs in the guide: /memory answers 'what was loaded', while @import and .claude/rules/ answer 'how should the content be organized'.

questions.prompt: A developer wants a personal shorthand command available in every repository on her machine, without committing anything to the team's repository. Where should it live?

options.text: In .claude/commands/ at the repository root, where it is picked up alongside the project's shared commands.
In ~/.claude/commands/, which holds user-scoped commands that are not shared with the team.
In the user-level CLAUDE.md, described in prose so Claude interprets it each time the command is used.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options covering the two command scopes the guide names plus the common mistake of trying to express a command as prose in CLAUDE.md.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing the project scope with the personal scope; .claude/commands/ is committed and shared, which is exactly what this developer is avoiding.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that slash commands are defined in markdown prose rather than in command or skill files.

explanation.correct: The guide distinguishes project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/, which are shared with the team via version control, from user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/, which are personal. For skills the equivalent escape hatch is to create personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ under different names, so teammates are unaffected.

whyWrong.a: .claude/commands/ is the project scope. Files there are shared through version control, so a personal command placed there would be committed and adopted by the whole team.
whyWrong.c: CLAUDE.md carries always-loaded instructions, not invocable command definitions. The command files in the commands and skills directories are what back a slash command.

explanation.takeaway: Shared with the team goes in .claude/commands/; stays personal goes in ~/.claude/commands/.
explanation.deepDive: The same two scopes apply to skills: project skills live in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files, while personal variants go in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names to avoid affecting teammates.

questions.prompt: A skill takes a target directory as a required argument, writes generated files under it, and must not run destructive commands. Which frontmatter configuration matches the guide's guidance?

options.text: context: fork only - running the skill in an isolated sub-agent means it needs no other frontmatter configuration.
allowed-tools limited to file write operations, plus argument-hint so the required directory is prompted for when the skill is invoked bare.
allowed-tools: Write, and nothing else - restricting tool access is the only configuration a skill's frontmatter carries.
A description field only - frontmatter configuration is limited to descriptive text about the skill.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, one per combination the scenario makes thinkable: isolate only, restrict destructive tools only, restrict destructive tools and prompt for the required argument, and the 'frontmatter is only metadata' misconception. Both required capabilities, allowed-tools and argument-hint, have to be in the same option, and the distractors each drop or replace one of them.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating context: fork as a substitute for the rest of the configuration; it decides where the skill's output goes, not what it needs or may do.
distractorRationale.b: Probes restricting tools but ignoring the required argument, and the belief that allowed-tools is the only field frontmatter offers.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that SKILL.md frontmatter is documentation-only rather than executable configuration.

explanation.correct: allowed-tools restricts tool access during skill execution, for example limiting it to file write operations to prevent destructive actions, which is what the scenario's no-destructive-commands requirement calls for. argument-hint prompts developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments, which is what supplies the target directory.

whyWrong.a: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its output does not pollute the main conversation. It neither prompts for a missing required parameter nor restricts which tools the skill may call, so it cannot deliver this skill's two requirements.
whyWrong.b: allowed-tools is right about the destructive-tool restriction but stops there. Without argument-hint a developer who invokes the skill without arguments gets no prompt for the required directory, and the guide supports context: fork and argument-hint alongside allowed-tools.
whyWrong.d: Frontmatter is configuration, not just documentation: context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint are all supported frontmatter options in a SKILL.md file.

explanation.takeaway: context: fork isolates a skill's noisy output, allowed-tools limits what it can do, argument-hint asks for missing parameters.
explanation.deepDive: Three frontmatter options carry three different jobs: context: fork for skills that produce verbose output or exploratory context such as codebase analysis or brainstorming alternatives, allowed-tools to bound which tools a skill may call while it runs, and argument-hint so the skill never has to guess a required input. Note what allowed-tools bounds: the set of tools, not the paths those tools may write to. A well-configured skill uses the options its use case calls for, which is not necessarily all three.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes skills from CLAUDE.md, as the guide presents them?

options.text: Skills are invoked on demand for task-specific workflows; CLAUDE.md supplies always-loaded universal standards.
CLAUDE.md is invoked on demand for task-specific workflows, while skills load automatically on every request.

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because this is a clean binary distinction with a single, memorable failure mode - swapping the loading behavior of the two mechanisms.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the exact inversion this objective tests: on-demand versus always-loaded, and skills versus CLAUDE.md.

explanation.correct: The guide states the choice plainly: skills are the on-demand mechanism for task-specific workflows, while CLAUDE.md holds the universal standards that are always loaded. That is the decision rule for whether a piece of guidance belongs in .claude/skills/ or in CLAUDE.md.

whyWrong.a: Both halves are reversed. CLAUDE.md is always loaded rather than invoked on demand, and skills wait for an explicit invocation rather than loading automatically.

explanation.takeaway: CLAUDE.md is always on; a skill waits until someone invokes it.
explanation.deepDive: The same personal-versus-team split shows up in customization: a developer can keep personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ under different names, so their own workflows do not affect teammates.

questions.prompt: Test files are spread across packages/web, packages/api, and packages/worker, and all of them must follow the same conventions. What does the guide recommend?

options.text: Add a separate CLAUDE.md file inside each of the three directories so the test conventions load per folder.
Create a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter paths such as ["**/*.test.tsx"] so it loads for test files.
Create a .claude/rules/ file with paths such as ["packages/**"] so the rule activates while editing package files.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the only real decision is how to scope one convention that must reach many directories: duplicate it per folder, glob the package tree, or glob the file type. Only the file-type glob satisfies the requirement.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the per-directory duplication that path-scoped rules exist to replace when a convention spans multiple directories.
distractorRationale.d: Probes writing a glob at the wrong level of specificity - packages/** matches every file under packages, so the rule would load for package source too.

explanation.correct: .claude/rules/ files support YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns. Glob patterns let a rule apply a convention to files by type regardless of directory location, so a pattern like **/*.test.tsx reaches every test file in the repository, which is exactly the situation described.

whyWrong.a: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files work per directory, which is precisely the limitation the guide says path-scoped rules overcome. Three copies of the same convention would also drift apart over time.
whyWrong.d: packages/** matches all files under packages, so the rule would activate while editing package source files as well as tests. The glob must target the test file type, not the package tree.

explanation.takeaway: When a convention spans directories, glob by file type in a .claude/rules/ paths field rather than copying it into each folder.
explanation.deepDive: The guide's Terraform example - paths: ["terraform/**/*"] - is the same idea narrowed to a subtree: one rule, one glob, stated once instead of once per folder.

questions.prompt: A repository adds a long, file-type-specific rule to .claude/rules/. According to the guide, when does that rule load, and what does that save?

options.text: Only while files matching its path pattern are edited, which reduces irrelevant context and token usage.
Whenever that file type is mentioned in a request, even if no matching file is being edited.
Once at session start, after which it stays resident for the whole session as project instructions.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options isolate the guide's stated trigger, files being edited, from the two plausible but undescribed triggers, topical mention in the request and unconditional session residency.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating path scoping as topical relevance: the guide keys activation to editing matching files, not to what the conversation mentions.
distractorRationale.c: Probes assuming rule files behave like always-loaded memory files, which removes the conditional loading that saves context.

explanation.correct: The guide states that path-scoped rules load only when matching files are edited, which reduces irrelevant context and token usage. The rule stays out of the way on unrelated work, and its detail costs nothing until the files it governs are actually being changed.

whyWrong.a: Activation is tied to editing files that match the pattern, not to the subject of the request. A conversation about Terraform that touches no Terraform file does not pull the rule in.
whyWrong.c: Rules that load once and remain for the whole session are exactly the always-loaded case. The guide's point is that a rule can be long and highly specific because it only appears when it is relevant.

explanation.takeaway: Path scoping is what lets a rule be long and specific: it costs context only while its files are being edited.
explanation.deepDive: This is the second half of the case for rules over duplicated files. The glob decides which files a convention governs; conditional loading decides how much that convention costs on every task that does not.

questions.prompt: Which task most clearly warrants plan mode before any code is written?

options.text: Choosing between integration approaches that carry different infrastructure requirements.
Any change that touches more than one file, since multi-file modification always requires plan mode first.
Fixing a single-file bug where the stack trace already points at the failing line.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the guide's own architectural example, its own direct-execution example, and the file-count shortcut misconception.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the rule-of-thumb version of the decision: file count instead of complexity, ambiguity, or architectural consequence.
distractorRationale.c: Probes under-using plan mode on a well-understood, tightly scoped fix that the guide explicitly places in direct execution.

explanation.correct: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications. Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements is exactly that kind of decision, and plan mode enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes.

whyWrong.a: Multi-file modification is one signal among several, not an automatic trigger. The guide describes combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation, so the deciding question is whether the approach is understood, not how many files change.
whyWrong.c: The guide names a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace as a case for direct execution: simple, well-scoped, and no design decision to explore first.

explanation.takeaway: Plan mode is for architectural decisions and genuinely competing approaches, not for every multi-file edit.
explanation.deepDive: The payoff the guide describes is preventing costly rework: exploring and designing before the first edit is cheap, while discovering the wrong architecture after dozens of files have changed is not.

questions.prompt: A migration task opens with a long discovery phase - reading dozens of affected files, cataloguing call sites, comparing options - and the main conversation keeps running low on context. What does the guide recommend?

options.text: Run the discovery in the main conversation and record the raw results in CLAUDE.md so they survive later sessions.
Skip discovery and start editing files directly, letting Claude infer the affected call sites from the stack trace.
Wrap the discovery in a custom skill with context: fork so its output is delivered back into the main session.
Use the Explore subagent to isolate the verbose discovery output and return a summary to the main conversation.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because three plausible context-management strategies exist - persist, skip, or isolate - and the reader must choose the one the guide credits with preserving main-conversation context.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating persistence as conservation; storing raw output in CLAUDE.md reloads it every session and spends more context, not less.
distractorRationale.b: Probes skipping the exploration phase that plan mode exists to provide, which is the route to the costly rework plan mode prevents.
distractorRationale.d: Probes misapplying the fork mechanism from skill frontmatter; forking moves output away from the main session rather than into it.

explanation.correct: The Explore subagent exists for isolating verbose discovery output and returning summaries, preserving the main conversation context during multi-phase tasks. The guide pairs it with plan mode: explore and design first, then execute the planned approach directly.

whyWrong.a: Recording raw discovery output in CLAUDE.md means every later session pays to re-read it. The guide's answer to verbose output is isolation, not storage.
whyWrong.b: Skipping discovery removes the safe exploration and design step, which is how a migration ends up needing rework. Plan mode exists precisely to explore before committing to changes.
whyWrong.d: context: fork runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation - which means a forked skill's output stays out of the main session rather than being delivered into it. Returning summaries to the main conversation is what the Explore subagent does.

explanation.takeaway: Verbose discovery belongs in the Explore subagent, and the plan belongs before the edits.
explanation.deepDive: Context isolation is a recurring theme in this domain: the Explore subagent for discovery phases, and context: fork for skills that produce verbose output such as codebase analysis or exploratory brainstorming.

questions.prompt: A developer needs to add a single validation check to one function whose behavior they already understand. Which mode should they use?

options.text: Plan mode, so the change is reviewed as a design before any implementation is written.
Direct execution, because the change is simple and its scope is already clear.

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the guide states the rule for this case directly; padding it with weaker variants would obscure the simple, well-scoped versus architectural split.

distractorRationale.a: Probes defaulting to the heavier process out of habit; the guide reserves plan mode for large-scale changes and multiple valid approaches.

explanation.correct: Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes, and the guide gives exactly this example - adding a date validation conditional - alongside a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace. Nothing about the approach is undecided, so a design phase adds cost without reducing risk.

whyWrong.a: Plan mode is designed for complex work: large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications. A single understood validation check has none of those properties.

explanation.takeaway: Well-understood, tightly scoped work goes straight to direct execution.
explanation.deepDive: The guide does not frame plan mode and direct execution as opposites to choose between once; it describes combining them - plan the library migration, then execute the approach that was planned.

questions.prompt: A developer describes a data transformation in prose and receives three slightly different implementations. What is the most effective fix, according to the guide?

options.text: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples so the expected transformation is pinned down unambiguously.
Write the test suite first, then iterate by sharing each test failure back to Claude one run at a time.
Restate the same description with more detail and ask Claude to choose the interpretation it considers most likely.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the guide's recommended fix, plus the two iterations - test-driven and prose-rewriting - that address the symptom rather than the ambiguity.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reaching for test-driven iteration when the requirement itself is underspecified; a failing test cannot tell you which of three transformations was intended.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the assumption that more words remove ambiguity, which is the exact failure mode - prose is what got interpreted inconsistently.

explanation.correct: Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. Two or three worked examples remove the interpretation step, because there is nothing left to infer.

whyWrong.a: Test-driven iteration - writing suites first and iterating by sharing failures - is part of the guide, but it is a way to refine against a failing suite. When the requirement itself is ambiguous, tests encode the wrong target.
whyWrong.c: Rewriting the same ambiguous prose keeps the ambiguity in place. The guide attributes inconsistent results precisely to natural-language descriptions being interpreted differently each time.

explanation.takeaway: Two or three concrete input/output examples beat a paragraph of prose.
explanation.deepDive: The same technique fixes edge cases: providing specific test cases with example input and expected output is how the guide suggests pinning down handling of values such as nulls in migration scripts.

questions.prompt: A review turned up several bugs. Which grouping matches the guide's guidance on how to deliver them?

options.text: Send every issue in a single message regardless of interaction, to minimize the number of turns.
Send one issue per message in every case, even when several fixes must agree on the same code.
Send interacting fixes together in one detailed message, and address independent issues sequentially.
Batch issues into one message only when they are fully independent of one another.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the guide's rule is a conditional pairing; the distractors cover batching-always, one-at-a-time-always, and the precise inversion of the condition.

distractorRationale.a: Probes batching by turn count rather than by dependency, which hides which fixes were meant to interact.
distractorRationale.b: Probes equating small increments with safety; the guide explicitly prefers a single message when the fixes interact.
distractorRationale.d: Probes inverting the condition so that independence, rather than interaction, is what justifies batching.

explanation.correct: The guide's rule is conditional: when fixes interact, provide them in a single detailed message so they are resolved against one another; when the problems are independent, fix them sequentially so each change can be judged on its own.

whyWrong.a: Batching everything regardless of interaction throws away the reason for the rule. Independent issues delivered together give no signal about which change resolved which problem.
whyWrong.b: Message count is not the deciding factor. The guide's condition is whether the fixes interact, and interacting fixes are meant to arrive together.
whyWrong.d: This reverses the rule: independent problems are the ones the guide advises handling sequentially, while interacting ones belong in one message.

explanation.takeaway: Interacting fixes go in one message; independent fixes go one at a time.
explanation.deepDive: The same judgment governs how test-driven iteration is delivered. The guide has you write the test suite first and then iterate by sharing test failures to guide progressive improvement, which is the habit of letting each response answer a specific, identified problem instead of a mixed batch of them.

questions.prompt: A developer asks Claude to add caching to a service they are unfamiliar with and is about to accept the first design that comes back. What does the guide suggest first?

options.text: Provide three input/output examples of cache hits and misses, since concrete examples always settle the design.
Skip the design phase and implement the simplest approach, then refine it later using test failures.
Have Claude ask questions first, so considerations such as cache invalidation and failure modes surface.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the guide's interview pattern, plus the two techniques the guide ties to other problems - examples for ambiguous transformations and tests for post-implementation iteration.

distractorRationale.a: Probes over-applying the examples technique; it resolves ambiguous transformations, not architectural questions like invalidation strategy.
distractorRationale.c: Probes skipping design in the domain the guide flags as most in need of questioning, which is where unanticipated failure modes bite.

explanation.correct: The interview pattern means having Claude ask questions before implementing, so considerations the developer may not have anticipated - cache invalidation strategies, failure modes - are surfaced while the solution is still cheap to change. The guide ties it to unfamiliar domains.

whyWrong.a: Concrete input/output examples are the guide's remedy for transformations described inconsistently in prose. A caching design is not a transformation spec, so examples would settle the wrong question.
whyWrong.c: Building first and refining with test failures inverts the guide's order. In an unfamiliar domain the interview pattern exists precisely because the failure modes are not yet visible, so they would not be caught by tests.

explanation.takeaway: In unfamiliar domains, let Claude interview you before it implements.
explanation.deepDive: The interview pattern is the discovery phase of iterative refinement; once the considerations are on the table, the guide's other tools - concrete examples, written tests, and failure-driven iteration - take over.

questions.prompt: Claude Code runs as a step in a CI job and the step hangs waiting on input that will never arrive. What is the fix?

options.text: Pass --output-format json so the pipeline receives a parseable response instead of blocking on input.
Invoke Claude Code with the -p (or --print) flag so it runs in non-interactive mode.
Remove CLAUDE.md from the repository so the run starts from a clean, empty context.
Add an argument-hint to the command definition so the pipeline knows which parameters to supply.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options separating the four CLI-adjacent levers the guide names - output formatting, project context, non-interactive mode, and argument hints - because only one addresses a hang on input.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing output shape with interactivity; json formatting says nothing about whether Claude waits for a human.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the belief that a leaner context prevents hangs, when CLAUDE.md is what gives CI runs their project context.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing the developer-facing argument-hint with pipeline behavior; it prompts a person typing a skill invocation, not a runner.

explanation.correct: The -p (or --print) flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode, which is what automated pipelines require. The guide names it specifically for preventing interactive input hangs in CI.

whyWrong.a: --output-format json controls the shape of the result, not whether Claude blocks for input. A job waiting on a prompt stays waiting no matter how the output is formatted.
whyWrong.b: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for providing project context - testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria - to CI-invoked Claude Code. Removing it makes the run less informed; it does not address the hang.
whyWrong.d: argument-hint prompts developers for required parameters when they invoke a skill without arguments. It is a prompting aid for humans, not a control over how a pipeline executes.

explanation.takeaway: -p / --print is the flag that keeps Claude Code non-interactive in CI.
explanation.deepDive: The other two CI flags solve a different problem: --output-format json with --json-schema enforce structured, machine-parseable findings so a pipeline can post them automatically as inline PR comments.

questions.prompt: A CI job must turn Claude Code's findings into automated inline PR comments. Which mechanism does the guide give?

options.text: -p alone, so the review runs without waiting for interactive input before producing comments.
--output-format json together with --json-schema, to produce machine-parseable structured findings.
A CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude to format its findings as JSON before it answers.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options contrasting the two flag families the guide introduces for CI - non-interactive execution versus structured output - plus a prose-based attempt to get the same result.

distractorRationale.a: Probes assuming any CI flag produces postable output; -p solves the hang, not the parsing.
distractorRationale.c: Probes treating CLAUDE.md as an output-formatting control when the guide assigns it the job of supplying project context.

explanation.correct: --output-format json and --json-schema are the CLI flags the guide names for enforcing structured output in CI contexts. With findings in a machine-parseable shape, a pipeline can post them automatically as inline PR comments.

whyWrong.a: -p makes the run non-interactive, which a pipeline needs, but it does not shape the output - there is still nothing guaranteed for the job to parse into comments.
whyWrong.c: CLAUDE.md's CI role is context: testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria. Asking in prose for a format is not the enforcement mechanism the guide identifies.

explanation.takeaway: Structured CI output comes from --output-format json plus --json-schema, not from prompting.
explanation.deepDive: The same CLAUDE.md content raises output quality in CI: documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures improves generated tests, and providing existing test files lets test generation avoid duplicating scenarios the suite already covers.

questions.prompt: A CI review job re-runs after every new commit and keeps posting the same findings again as duplicate comments. What does the guide recommend?

options.text: Clear the job's stored history before each run, so every review starts from a context-free baseline.
Include prior review findings in context and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues.

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the guide names one specific remedy for duplicate comments on re-run reviews; adding weaker variants would dilute the recall target.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the instinct to reset state on duplicate output, when the duplicates are caused by re-reporting known findings rather than by stale stored state.

explanation.correct: When re-running reviews after new commits, include the prior review findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. That preserves what is already known while still letting genuinely unresolved problems resurface.

whyWrong.a: Wiping history would remove the very information needed to suppress duplicates. It also discards the record of which findings were already raised, so unresolved issues could be lost rather than repeated.

explanation.takeaway: Feed prior findings back in, then ask only for new or still-unaddressed issues.
explanation.deepDive: This is a context-design decision rather than a filter: the reviewer is told what it already said, so its second output is a delta rather than a replay.

questions.prompt: Which setup does the guide recommend for the automated review that runs on a pull request?

options.text: Let Claude write the code and review it in the same session, so it reasons from full knowledge of the intent.
Review in a fresh session with CLAUDE.md removed, to avoid anchoring the reviewer on project conventions.
Use an independent review instance, since the session that wrote the code reviews its own work less effectively.
Start a fresh review instance but seed it with a summary of the generator's reasoning, so it knows the original intent.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options for a misconception the guide names explicitly, plus three realistic attempts to obtain a good review without actually isolating it from the generating session.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the intuition that more context from the authoring session makes a better reviewer - the exact effect the guide calls out as reduced.
distractorRationale.b: Probes stripping context as a way to gain independence; independence comes from a separate instance, not from deleting project standards.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating a new session as sufficient separation. The guide's independence is defined by the absence of the generator's reasoning context, which a summary reintroduces.

explanation.correct: Session context isolation is the guide's point for CI review: the same Claude session that generated the code is less effective at reviewing its own changes than an independent review instance would be. CLAUDE.md supplies the project context the independent reviewer needs - testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria.

whyWrong.a: This is the misconception the guide names. Reusing the generating session reduces the value of the review rather than improving it, no matter how well that session understands the intent.
whyWrong.b: Removing CLAUDE.md strips the review of the criteria it is supposed to check against. Independence is achieved with a separate instance, not by deleting project context.
whyWrong.d: A fresh instance is only independent while it lacks the generator's reasoning. A summary of that reasoning reintroduces the same committed explanation of the choices, so the reviewer inherits the blind spot the guide is trying to remove.

explanation.takeaway: Review with a fresh, independent instance - not the session that generated the code.
explanation.deepDive: Combine the pieces for a complete CI review: -p for non-interactive execution, --output-format json with --json-schema for machine-parseable findings, CLAUDE.md for project context, and prior findings in context so re-runs report only new or still-unaddressed issues.

questions.prompt: A code-review prompt tells Claude to "check that comments are accurate." Which revision applies the guidance the guide recommends most directly?

options.text: Be conservative: only report comments you are highly confident are wrong.
Flag comments only when the claimed behavior contradicts the actual code behavior.
Only report findings you judge to be high confidence, and stay silent otherwise.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options isolate one contrast: the vague-instruction pattern versus the explicit, categorical criterion. A fourth would repeat the same vague phrasing rather than test a new distinction.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that general conservatism language ("be conservative") sharpens review precision.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the same confidence-filtering misconception in a second phrasing, showing it is a pattern rather than one awkward sentence.

explanation.correct: The guide contrasts "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior" with "check that comments are accurate" — the former states a specific, checkable condition rather than a goal.

whyWrong.a: "Be conservative" is exactly the general-instruction pattern the guide says fails to improve precision; it never defines which comments are reportable.
whyWrong.c: Confidence filtering changes how many findings surface without defining reportable categories, so precision stays inconsistent across runs.

explanation.analogy: Asking for "accurate comments" is like telling a reviewer to find "good bugs"; asking for comments that contradict the code gives a condition you can actually check.
explanation.takeaway: State the reportable condition explicitly; vague goals and confidence filters do not raise precision.
explanation.deepDive: The same principle applies to every review category: define what to report (bugs, security) versus what to skip (minor style, local patterns) instead of relying on confidence-based filtering.

questions.prompt: A team adds the instruction "only report high-confidence findings" to its review prompt and precision does not improve. How does the guide explain that outcome?

options.text: High-confidence wording only changes whether a finding is labeled an error or a warning in the output schema.
It filters findings by the model's own confidence rather than defining which issue categories to report versus skip.
It makes the model report every issue it notices, so that nothing is silently dropped.
It replaces categorical severity levels with a single pass-or-fail verdict for each file.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options here each encode a different and common misconception about what a confidence instruction is supposed to do, and only one matches the guide's mechanism.

distractorRationale.a: Confuses prompt wording with output formatting: it treats the instruction as a labeling change rather than a filtering rule.
distractorRationale.b: Inverts the effect of the instruction, which suppresses uncertain findings rather than flooding the review.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that collapsing to a single verdict is a valid simplification of severity classification.

explanation.correct: The guide names "be conservative" and "only report high-confidence findings" as general instructions that fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria, because they filter on confidence instead of on category.

whyWrong.a: Severity labels come from the criteria you define; the confidence sentence does not relabel anything, it only gates what gets reported at all.
whyWrong.b: The instruction reduces output volume. Reporting everything is the opposite of what "only report high-confidence findings" asks for.
whyWrong.d: The guide calls for explicit severity criteria with concrete examples per level, not a single binary verdict that erases severity.

explanation.analogy: Confidence filtering is a volume knob. Category criteria are a specification.
explanation.takeaway: Confidence wording filters output; explicit category criteria are what actually raise precision.

questions.prompt: One review category keeps producing findings developers dismiss as noise, and trust in the accurate categories is now slipping. What does the guide recommend?

options.text: Temporarily disable that category while its prompt is improved, then bring it back.
Lower the severity threshold across every category so the noisy findings blend into the rest.
Leave it enabled but attach a confidence score to each finding and filter on that score.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options cover the three plausible responses a team actually considers: retune everything, switch off the category, or filter it by confidence.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the reflex to tune the whole system to hide one bad category, which degrades the categories that were working.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confidence-based remedy the guide already rejects in 4.1.

explanation.correct: The guide lists temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while prompts for those categories are improved.

whyWrong.a: Lowering severity globally does not remove the false positives; it demotes genuinely important findings in the categories developers still trust.
whyWrong.c: Confidence-based filtering was already shown not to improve precision, so leaving the category on keeps the noise in the review.

explanation.takeaway: A noisy category costs you trust in every other category, so switch it off, fix the prompt, then re-enable.

questions.prompt: According to the guide, when is few-shot prompting the most effective technique?

options.text: When a task is fully deterministic and the same output can be computed without a model.
When detailed instructions alone yield inconsistent formatting and the output must be reliably actionable.
When the source documents are long enough that they will not fit within the context window.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options test the trigger condition for few-shot against two plausible but wrong framings (no model needed, or a context-window problem).

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that few-shot is a general quality lever even when the task does not need a model.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between formatting inconsistency and context exhaustion.

explanation.correct: The guide calls few-shot examples the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results.

whyWrong.a: If the output can be computed deterministically, examples are not the lever; the guide ties few-shot to inconsistency caused by instructions, not to task type.
whyWrong.c: Few-shot examples demonstrate output format and judgment; they are not a remedy for documents that exceed the context window.

explanation.takeaway: Reach for few-shot when your instructions are precise but the output still comes back inconsistent.

questions.prompt: The guide recommends 2-4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous cases such as tool selection. What should each example actually show?

options.text: The ambiguous request, the chosen action, and the reasoning for why it beat plausible alternatives.
A catalog of every request pattern seen so far, each mapped to the action that matched it.
The final answer only, so the model copies the output shape without inheriting any reasoning.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options separate the three candidate designs for a few-shot example: enumeration, reasoning, and bare output — the distinctions the guide actually draws.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that few-shot examples are a lookup table of enumerated cases rather than demonstrations of judgment.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that format-only examples suffice; the guide ties examples to demonstrating reasoning over plausible alternatives.

explanation.correct: The guide asks for 2-4 targeted examples for ambiguous scenarios that show the reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.

whyWrong.a: A catalog teaches pattern matching over pre-specified cases; the guide emphasizes that examples should let the model generalize judgment to novel patterns.
whyWrong.c: Answer-only examples reproduce the surface format but leave the ambiguous-case decision to guesswork, which is exactly what the guide wants demonstrated.

explanation.takeaway: Few-shot examples must show the decision and its justification, not just the finished answer.

questions.prompt: An extraction pipeline returns empty or null required fields on documents whose formatting varies. Which few-shot addition does the guide point to?

options.text: An exhaustive enumeration of every document layout the extractor might ever encounter.
Many copies of one perfectly formatted document, reinforcing a single expected layout.
Examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats and structures.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options map directly onto the guide's failure mode: enumerating cases, demonstrating varied formats, or reinforcing one format.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that more exhaustive case coverage is the fix, when the guide wants examples that generalize across formats.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that repeating one clean example handles format variance, which is the opposite of what the examples are for.

explanation.correct: The guide recommends few-shot examples demonstrating correct handling of varied document structures — for example inline citations versus bibliographies, or methodology sections versus embedded details — to address empty or null extraction of required fields.

whyWrong.a: An exhaustive enumeration still teaches matching pre-specified cases, and it fails on the novel layouts that caused the empty extractions.
whyWrong.c: One repeated layout teaches nothing about the other structures, so the null fields on varied documents remain.

explanation.analogy: The model needs to see that a citation can live in a bibliography or inline, not memorize the bibliography case.
explanation.takeaway: To fix null extractions, show examples across varied document structures, not more instructions.

questions.prompt: An ingestion service defines extract_invoice, extract_purchase_order, and extract_manifest, and it cannot tell in advance which of them a request needs. Which tool_choice setting does the guide prescribe?

options.text: "any", which guarantees structured output when several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown.
"auto", leaving it to the model to weigh the schema descriptions and decide whether a tool is needed.
A forced tool by name, so that every document is pinned to one extraction schema and compliance never varies.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options separate the setting the guide pairs with the unknown-document-type case from the two alternatives a reader is likely to reach for, a model-judged choice and a pinned single tool.

distractorRationale.a: Probes trusting "auto" because the schemas are well described, forgetting that auto still permits a plain text answer instead of a tool call.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for a pinned tool as the strongest guarantee, when the document type is precisely what is not known.

explanation.correct: The guide pairs "any" with this exact situation: setting tool_choice to "any" guarantees structured output when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown. The model chooses among the available schemas, and every branch still returns a schema-compliant result.

whyWrong.a: "auto" leaves the decision to call a tool to the model, which means it may reply in conversational text instead. That is the gap "any" closes in this scenario.
whyWrong.c: Forcing a tool by name pins one extraction, which only helps when you already know which extraction to run. Here the document type is unknown, so pinning one schema discards the other two.

explanation.takeaway: Several extraction schemas and an unknown document type is the "any" case; forcing a named tool is the opposite situation.
explanation.deepDive: Choosing "any" removes the need for a classification step of your own. The model arbitrates between the available schemas, so the guarantee of a schema-compliant response holds on every branch rather than depending on your guess about the document.

questions.prompt: Extraction runs through a tool with a strict JSON schema, yet invoices arrive where line items sum to $400 while the total field says $500. What did the schema actually guarantee?

options.text: That every required field holds a value actually extracted from the source document.
Only the syntax and shape: strict schemas remove JSON syntax errors but not semantic errors.
That values land in the semantically correct field, since field names constrain content.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options separate the two error classes the guide draws a hard line between: syntax, and everything semantic.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the overclaim that schema validation means the content is faithful to the source.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that field names enforce meaning, which is exactly the semantic check a schema cannot perform.

explanation.correct: The guide states that strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors such as line items that do not sum to the total, or values placed in the wrong field.

whyWrong.a: A required field only guarantees a value is present, not that the value came from the document rather than being inferred or fabricated.
whyWrong.c: Field naming guides the model but cannot verify that a value belongs in that field; that check belongs in a validation step.

explanation.analogy: A strict schema is a grammar check. It guarantees well-formed sentences, not that the facts in them add up.
explanation.takeaway: Strict schemas guarantee well-formed JSON, never correct content.
explanation.deepDive: This is why format normalization rules still belong in the prompt alongside a strict schema, and why semantic checks such as total reconciliation are layered on afterwards.

questions.prompt: An extraction tool must return a policy_limit field, but many source documents never state a limit. Which schema design does the guide recommend?

options.text: Keep the field required and tell the model to estimate a value whenever the document omits one.
Keep the field required and constrain it to an enum of "unclear" and "other" with a detail string.
Make the field optional or nullable so the model can return nothing instead of inventing a value.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options capture the realistic design choices for a field the source may not contain: required with an instruction, nullable, or enum-escaped.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that completeness of the output matters more than faithfulness to the source, inviting fabrication.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between enum patterns for extensible categories and nullability for absent values.

explanation.correct: The guide says to design schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, which prevents the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields.

whyWrong.a: A required field with an instruction to estimate invites exactly the fabrication the nullable design prevents.
whyWrong.c: Enum values such as "unclear" and "other" plus a detail field serve extensible categorization; a numeric limit that is simply absent needs nullability.

explanation.takeaway: If the source may not contain it, make the field nullable — required fields invite fabrication.
explanation.deepDive: The enum pattern still matters elsewhere: add "unclear" for ambiguous cases and "other" plus a detail string when a category list must stay extensible.

questions.prompt: A triage schema sorts findings into a fixed set of categories, and new categories keep appearing that the enum does not cover. Which change does the guide recommend?

options.text: Add enum values such as "unclear" for ambiguous cases and "other" plus a detail field.
Extend the enum each time a new category appears and redeploy the schema after every update.
Replace the enum with a free-text string so the model can describe any category it finds.
Add a second required category field so each finding can be placed in two existing buckets.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, because an enum designed for fixed values has several genuinely tempting wrong answers: grow it, drop it, or double it.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that a schema must be rewritten to stay accurate instead of designed to absorb novelty.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that flexibility requires abandoning constraint, losing the schema compliance tool use provides.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the idea that overloading a finding across buckets solves the missing-category problem.

explanation.correct: The guide calls for enum fields with "other" plus a detail string for extensible categories, and enum values like "unclear" for ambiguous cases, so the schema absorbs categories you did not anticipate.

whyWrong.a: Continuously extending the enum turns every surprise into a schema change; the "other" plus detail pattern is the extensibility mechanism.
whyWrong.c: Free text removes the structured guarantee that motivated using a schema at all.
whyWrong.d: Requiring two categories creates ambiguity about which is authoritative and still cannot name a category outside the list.

explanation.takeaway: Design enums with "unclear" and "other" plus a detail field so new categories do not break the schema.

questions.prompt: A validation check rejects an extraction. What makes a retry most likely to produce a corrected result?

options.text: Resend the original request unchanged, on the theory that the failure came from output variance.
Resend a shortened prompt that omits the failed output and asks for a cleaner answer.
Resend the request several times and accept the first result that satisfies the schema.
Resend the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options contrast error-feedback retries against the three lazy alternatives teams reach for when a validator fails.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that a rejection is random noise that a plain resend will clear.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the idea that trimming context helps, when the retry needs the failed attempt and the specific errors.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating retries as repeated sampling rather than a correction loop.

explanation.correct: Retry-with-error-feedback means appending specific validation errors to the prompt on retry, and the guide's follow-up requests include the original document, the failed extraction, and those specific errors so the model can self-correct.

whyWrong.a: Without the validation errors the model has no signal about what was wrong, so an unchanged resend just repeats the failure.
whyWrong.b: Removing the failed extraction discards the very artifact the model needs to correct.
whyWrong.d: Sampling until the schema passes discards the error detail that would let the model fix the underlying problem.

explanation.takeaway: A retry must carry the document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors.
explanation.deepDive: Retries pay off for format mismatches and structural output errors. They fail when the required information is simply absent from the source.

questions.prompt: An extraction returns empty required fields for documents that reference a value held only in an external system that was never provided. What does the guide say about retrying?

options.text: Retry with the validation error appended, because the requirement will push the model to find the value.
Retry repeatedly with chunking, because the value is always present but out of context.
Retries will not help, because the information is absent from the source document that was provided.
Retry once with a broadened prompt, because broadening the prompt restores missing source data.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options test whether the learner can classify a failure as fixable (format or structure) or unfixable (information not present), which is the guide's central retry distinction.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that stronger error feedback can extract information the model never had.
distractorRationale.b: Probes misclassifying an absent-information failure as a context-window problem.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the idea that a broader prompt manufactures source data.

explanation.correct: The guide states retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source document, such as information that exists only in an external document that was not provided.

whyWrong.a: Error feedback corrects format and structure; it cannot supply a value the source never contained.
whyWrong.b: Chunking addresses documents too large for the context window, not fields whose value does not exist in the input.
whyWrong.d: Broadening a prompt changes how the model reads the document, not what the document contains.

explanation.takeaway: Retry fixes format and structure errors; it cannot fix information that was never in the input.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which are validation and feedback loop designs the guide describes?

options.text: Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and add conflict_detected booleans to flag discrepancies.
Add detected_pattern fields to structured findings so dismissed findings can be analyzed by pattern.
Route low-confidence findings to humans and drop the explicit report-versus-skip criteria.
Retry every failed document until it returns a value for each required field.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: two endorsed designs and two wrong ones, where the third discards the explicit report-versus-skip criteria that objective 4.1 requires and the fourth repeats the retry-limits misconception, so a learner cannot select both correct options by pattern alone.

distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that some substitute signal can stand in for written review criteria. Objective 4.1 asks for criteria that state which issues to report versus which to skip, and this option is wrong precisely because it drops them.
distractorRationale.d: Reuses the retry-limits misconception: retrying cannot conjure absent information.

explanation.correct: The guide describes both self-correction flows (extracting calculated_total alongside stated_total, and adding conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent source data) and feedback loop design via detected_pattern fields on structured findings to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns.

whyWrong.c: The second half is the failure. Objective 4.1 asks for review criteria written out explicitly, stating which issues to report and which to skip, and this option deletes exactly that requirement instead of supplying it.
whyWrong.d: The guide is explicit that retries are ineffective when the required information is absent from the source document.

explanation.analogy: calculated_total is an audit against stated_total; detected_pattern is a complaint tracker for the reviewer.
explanation.takeaway: Validate semantically with calculated-versus-stated totals, and track dismissed findings with detected_pattern.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the Message Batches API as this guide characterizes it?

options.text: A 50% cheaper path that commits to a guaranteed completion time, so pipelines can rely on it.
A 50% cheaper path that supports multi-turn tool calling inside a single request, returning tool results mid-request.
A 50% cheaper path in which custom_id values force batch responses to be returned in submission order.
A 50% cheaper path with an up-to-24-hour processing window and no guaranteed latency SLA.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because each of the batch API's four headline characteristics is a plausible mix-up: SLA, tool calling, the 24-hour window, and custom_id.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the invented guarantee that a 50% discount implies a committed completion time.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the belief that batching preserves multi-turn tool calling within one request.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the misconception that custom_id is an ordering mechanism rather than a correlation key.

explanation.correct: The guide describes the Message Batches API as offering 50% cost savings with an up-to-24-hour processing window and no guaranteed latency SLA.

whyWrong.a: There is no guaranteed latency SLA, which is exactly why batch work is restricted to latency-tolerant workloads.
whyWrong.b: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request; it cannot execute tools mid-request and return results.
whyWrong.d: custom_id fields exist to correlate batch request and response pairs, not to order results.

explanation.takeaway: Batches are 50% cheaper, may take up to 24 hours, and guarantee no latency.
explanation.deepDive: Because there is no guaranteed SLA, submission frequency is calculated against SLA constraints, for example 4-hour windows to guarantee a 30-hour SLA with 24-hour batch processing.

questions.prompt: A CI pipeline runs a blocking pre-merge security check on every push. Which API approach fits, and why?

options.text: Message Batches API, because 50% cost savings make the wait acceptable at merge time.
Synchronous API, because a blocking check cannot wait on an up-to-24-hour batch window.
Message Batches API submitted every 4 hours, to guarantee a 30-hour SLA across the merge timeout.
Message Batches API for the check, with a synchronous call used only to show a pending status.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options cover the realistic CI design debates: discount vs latency, batched-with-SLA-arithmetic, and asynchronous-with-a-wait-screen.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that cost savings outweigh a blocking workflow's latency requirement.
distractorRationale.c: Probes misapplying the guide's batch SLA arithmetic to a merge gate; a 30-hour guarantee is meaningless against a merge timeout.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the idea that deferring the check to a batch still makes it a pre-merge gate.

explanation.correct: The guide maps API choice to workflow latency: synchronous for blocking pre-merge checks, batch for overnight or weekly analysis, because batch processing is inappropriate for blocking workflows.

whyWrong.a: Batch processing is explicitly called out as inappropriate for blocking workflows such as pre-merge checks.
whyWrong.c: The 4-hour window and 30-hour SLA arithmetic assumes a latency-tolerant schedule; the result is still far beyond any merge gate.
whyWrong.d: Showing a pending status does not satisfy a blocking check; the merge would proceed without the security result.

explanation.takeaway: Blocking pre-merge checks are synchronous; batch is for work that can wait overnight or for a week.

questions.prompt: Half the documents in an overnight batch fail to process. What does the guide recommend?

options.text: Resubmit the entire batch, because partial resubmission would duplicate results already collected.
Prompt-refine on the failing subset and resubmit those, leaving oversized documents unchanged.
Resubmit only the failed documents, identified by custom_id, chunking any that exceeded context limits.
Wait for the next scheduled run, since failed items cannot be identified after a batch completes.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because partial resubmission, targeted prompt refinement, and blind full resubmission are all defensible-looking responses to the same incident.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that batch results are not individually addressable, when custom_id makes them so.
distractorRationale.b: Probes a half-right answer: prompt refinement helps first-pass success but is not a substitute for fixing the cause named in the guide.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that failed items cannot be located, which contradicts the role of custom_id.

explanation.correct: The guide says to handle batch failures by resubmitting only the failed documents, identified by custom_id, with appropriate modifications such as chunking documents that exceeded context limits.

whyWrong.a: custom_id exists precisely so a resubmission targets only the failures rather than re-paying for successful documents.
whyWrong.b: Prompt refinement on a sample set before batch processing maximizes first-pass success rates; it does not fix documents that already exceeded context limits.
whyWrong.d: custom_id correlates request and response pairs, which is how failed documents are identified.

explanation.takeaway: Batch failures are handled surgically: find them by custom_id and fix the actual cause, such as chunking.

questions.prompt: A team wants the generating session to catch its own mistakes, and proposes two fixes: tell it to review its own work more carefully, and give it extended thinking. What does the guide say?

options.text: Neither substitutes for an independent review instance, which the guide ranks above both.
Extended thinking alone is enough, since re-checking the same reasoning in more depth catches what the first pass missed.
Both are endorsed substitutes, and the guide treats them as equivalent to an independent instance.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the guide names exactly two substitutes to rank against an independent review instance - self-review instructions and extended thinking - plus one option that misreads the guide as putting all three on equal footing.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the belief that more reasoning depth inside the generating session recovers what self-review loses.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reading the guide as listing three interchangeable options rather than ranking one above the other two.

explanation.correct: The guide ranks independent review instances, which carry none of the generator's prior reasoning context, above two named substitutes: self-review instructions and extended thinking. Both are described as less effective at catching subtle issues than a separate instance.

whyWrong.b: Extended thinking is one of the two things an independent instance is ranked above, not a repair for self-review. Re-reading the same reasoning more carefully keeps the reasoning in place.
whyWrong.c: The guide does not put the three on equal footing. It says independent instances are more effective than self-review instructions or extended thinking, which is a ranking, not a menu of equivalents.

explanation.analogy: Asking someone to reread their own paragraph carefully is not the same as handing it to a fresh reader; more time with the same reasoning is still the same reasoning.
explanation.takeaway: Self-review instructions and extended thinking both rank below an instance that never saw the reasoning.

questions.prompt: A change spans 200 files and must be reviewed end to end. Which review architecture does the guide recommend?

options.text: Per-file local analysis passes plus separate cross-file integration passes for data flow.
One instance reading all files in a single pass, so every finding comes from a consistent voice.
A second instance reviewing only the generator's final answer text, without opening the files.
One integration pass across the whole change, leaving local checks to the developer's own review.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the single-pass, text-only, and integration-only architectures are all realistic proposals that fail for different reasons.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that one big pass keeps findings consistent, which is the attention dilution the guide warns about.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the belief that reviewing the answer text substitutes for an independent pass over the code itself.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that cross-file analysis alone suffices, dropping the focused local passes.

explanation.correct: The guide recommends multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings.

whyWrong.a: A single pass over 200 files dilutes attention and produces contradictory findings, which is what the multi-pass design exists to prevent.
whyWrong.b: Reviewing the generator's final answer text is not a review of the code. The multi-pass design splits the actual files into per-file local passes and separate cross-file integration passes.
whyWrong.d: Local and integration passes are complementary; dropping the local passes leaves local issues unexamined.

explanation.takeaway: Split large reviews into per-file passes plus cross-file integration passes.

questions.prompt: A team adds a verification pass in which Claude reports a confidence score alongside each finding and routes low-confidence findings to humans. How does the guide view this?

options.text: It is the recommended replacement for explicit report-versus-skip criteria, because scores are more objective.
It is invalid: the guide permits confidence only inside few-shot examples, never in review output.
It is a supported pattern for calibrated review routing, but it does not replace explicit criteria.
It is valid only on an independent instance, because a generator cannot assess its own confidence.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because self-reported confidence is a subtle cross-domain point: 4.6 endorses it for routing while 4.1 rejects it as a precision mechanism.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the overreach that turns a routing aid into a substitute for the explicit criteria from 4.1.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the misreading that the guide forbids confidence reporting, when it describes exactly such verification passes.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that confidence scores are only valid on an independent instance, which the guide does not attach to this pattern.

explanation.correct: The guide lists verification passes where the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing, while 4.1 states that general confidence instructions do not improve precision the way specific categorical criteria do.

whyWrong.a: Confidence routing is for deciding what a human looks at; precision still comes from criteria that define which issues to report versus skip.
whyWrong.b: The guide explicitly describes verification passes with self-reported confidence, so this overstates the restriction.
whyWrong.d: The guide attaches no independence condition to this pattern; verification passes that self-report confidence are listed as a review design in their own right.

explanation.takeaway: Self-reported confidence is a routing signal, not a substitute for explicit report-versus-skip criteria.

questions.prompt: A support agent summarizes earlier turns before each new prompt. What is the primary risk of that practice?

options.text: The summary keeps shrinking until the agent can no longer follow the thread.
The model reads summarized text less reliably than the original transcript.
Condensing turns drops exact details such as amounts, dates, and order numbers.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options isolate the fidelity failure the guide names (numbers, dates, percentages, expectations becoming vague) from two plausible but distinct confusions: pure length loss and model readability.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that the danger is losing the narrative thread rather than losing precise transactional values.
distractorRationale.c: Probes a processing-reliability theory of summarization; the guide attributes the damage to what the condensation omits, not to how summaries are read.

explanation.correct: The guide's stated risk of progressive summarization is that condensing numerical values, percentages, dates, and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries removes exactly the facts a support case turns on.

whyWrong.a: Compression is not the failure mode described. The problem is that summaries replace specific values with vague language, not that the conversation thread becomes unreadable.
whyWrong.c: Nothing in the guide says summaries are read unreliably. The loss occurs at write time, when details are omitted, so no reading strategy recovers them.

explanation.takeaway: Summarize the narrative; keep the numbers, dates, and order identifiers outside the summary.
explanation.analogy: A running log that says "the customer disputed a charge of about forty dollars last month" is useless for issuing the exact refund the case requires.
explanation.deepDive: The same warning applies to customer-stated expectations. "The customer was unhappy about delivery" loses the stated commitment ("it had to arrive before the 14th") that later decides the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which change most directly protects transactional accuracy across a long support session?

options.text: Extract amounts, dates, order numbers, and statuses into a case facts block.
Ask the customer to restate the order number and total at the start of each session.
Summarize the history progressively and check the details once at the end.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the correct pattern, a detect-late strategy that cannot recover dropped facts, and a workaround that pushes the cost back to the customer.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that accuracy can be restored by re-collecting facts interactively instead of persisting them in the architecture.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that an end-of-session accuracy check repairs summarization losses; the details are already gone by then.

explanation.correct: The guide's skill is to extract transactional facts into a persistent case facts block that is included in each prompt, outside summarized history, so amounts, dates, order numbers, and statuses survive every compression step.

whyWrong.a: Re-asking the customer does not fix the context design problem, and the guide's remedy is a separate context layer the agent controls.
whyWrong.b: A final check runs against a summary that has already lost the values; checking later cannot recreate the precise figure.

explanation.takeaway: Transactional facts belong in a persistent block carried in every prompt, not in summarized history.
explanation.deepDive: The companion skill for multi-issue sessions is the same idea generalized: extract and persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) into a separate context layer so one thread's compression cannot corrupt another's facts.

questions.prompt: A synthesis agent receives many subagent reports concatenated into one long input. How should the architect reduce position effects?

options.text: Move the summaries to the end of the input and drop the section headers.
Keep one continuous block and trust the model's preference for recent input.
Place key findings summaries at the start and label detail sections explicitly.
Trim each report down to a few sentences first, so the aggregate stops counting as a long input.

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options are justified because the practical alternatives people actually try (end placement, recency reliance, shrinking the aggregate) are all realistic and each probes a different wrong theory of position.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the half-right belief that the end of the input is as safe as the beginning, while discarding the section headers the guide pairs with it.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the assumption that recency weighting makes middle content safe; the lost-in-the-middle effect is precisely that middle findings get omitted.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating the lost-in-the-middle effect as an input-size problem that shrinking solves, when it is a position problem that structure solves.
